title: Which of these are connected?

prereqs.why: The definition, and the disconnecting pair of open sets, is what decides four of the five.
The classification of connected subsets of the line is what makes two of them immediate.
A continuous image of a connected space is connected, which is the cheapest argument for the circle.

statement:
A metric space is **disconnected** if it is the union of two disjoint
non-empty sets, both open in it. **Connected** means not disconnected.

Each subset below carries the metric inherited from the Euclidean space it
sits in, except where another metric is named. Select every one that is
**connected**.
hints: For a subset of $\R$ there is a complete answer: it is connected exactly when it is an interval. Two of these are subsets of $\R$.
To show a set is disconnected, exhibit the two open sets. For $[0,1] \cup (2,3]$, the obvious choice works.
The circle is the image of $[0, 2\pi]$ under the continuous map $t \mapsto (\cos t, \sin t)$, and a continuous image of a connected space is connected.
The topologist's sine curve is the graph of $\sin(1/x)$ for $x > 0$ together with the segment $\{0\} \times [-1,1]$. It is the standard example of a space that is connected and not path connected.

options: The topologist's sine curve: $\bigl\{(x, \sin(1/x)) : 0 < x \le 1\bigr\} \cup \bigl(\{0\} \times [-1,1]\bigr)$ in $\R^2$.
